question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a clinic or hospital?

options.A: To generate huge profits for hospital management
options.B: To store expired medications safely before disposal
options.C: To maintain a continuous and steady supply of essential drugs
options.D: To provide free medical treatment to all citizens

explanation: You've got this! The whole point of a DRF is to make sure essential medicines never run out. Money collected from sales is used right away to buy fresh stock. Simple and effective! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why is this special fund called 'revolving'?

options.A: Prices of medicines rotate every week based on inflation
options.B: Doctors take turns managing the pharmacy key
options.C: Patients return unsold drugs to get their money back
options.D: Money from drug sales is used to purchase replacement stock

explanation: Think of it as a cycle! Cash turns into drugs, drugs turn into cash, and the process keeps turning or 'revolving' so the pharmacy always has stock. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a main objective of the DRF system?

options.C: Providing free healthcare services to everyone

explanation: Spot on if you picked free healthcare! DRF drugs are sold at affordable, subsidized rates—not given away for free—so the fund can keep running. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h2)

question: How does the DRF system help protect patients from fake or substandard drugs?

options.A: By testing every single pill in a laboratory before selling it
options.B: By destroying all imported medications immediately
options.C: By purchasing drugs only from verified and approved suppliers
options.D: By allowing patients to bring their own drugs from home

explanation: Safety first! By sticking to trusted, approved suppliers, the pharmacy keeps fake medications far away from our patients. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h2)

question: What does it mean when a Drug Revolving Fund is described as 'ring-fenced'?

options.A: The pharmacy door must be locked with a special metal ring
options.B: Drugs are arranged in circular shelves inside the store
options.C: Profits are shared equally among all clinical department heads
options.D: Money from drug sales is kept separate and used only to buy more drugs

explanation: Ring-fencing is like putting a protective fence around the money. It ensures drug funds aren't mistakenly used to pay for other hospital bills! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h3)

question: Why is a small markup added to the cost price of DRF drugs?

options.A: To punish patients who buy drugs late in the evening
options.B: To make the hospital pharmacy richer than private stores
options.C: To pay bonuses to nurses on night shift duty
options.D: To cover minor operational costs and protect against inflation

explanation: That tiny extra amount isn't for profit—it helps cover transport costs and keeps the fund strong against rising prices. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h3)

question: In pharmacy inventory management, what does the rule 'FIFO' stand for?
explanation: Easy to remember: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) means the drugs that arrived first should be the ones dispensed first! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h4)

question: As a nurse, you receive new paracetamol expiring in 2026, but the shelf already has stock expiring in 2025. What should you do?

options.A: Place the 2025 stock in front and dispense it before the 2026 stock
options.B: Mix all the tablets together in one big container
options.C: Return both supplies immediately to the central medical store
options.D: Place the 2026 stock in front and keep the 2025 stock behind

explanation: Great clinical habit! Always use the ones expiring sooner (2025) so nothing spoils on the shelf. That's true nursing resourcefulness. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h4)

question: Why should nurses always advise patients not to keep leftover antibiotics for later use?

options.A: It increases the financial profit of the hospital
options.B: It causes the plastic containers to lose their shape
options.C: It encourages drug resistance and improper self-medication
options.D: It makes the pharmacy run out of receipt paper

explanation: Incomplete doses are a major driver of antibiotic resistance. Patient education here saves lives down the line! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h5)

question: What crucial checks must a nurse perform right before handing medication to a patient?

options.A: The political affiliation of the patient
options.B: Patient allergies and correct dosage instructions
options.C: The brand of the car the patient drove toanteen
options.D: The personal phone number of the prescribing doctor

explanation: Patient safety is job number one! Always double-check allergies and doses to prevent adverse drug reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h5)

question: Which of these is a major threat that can crash a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Issuing drugs on informal credit to friends and colleagues
options.B: Keeping the pharmacy windows open for ventilation
options.C: Writing clear dosage instructions on drug packs
options.D: Conducting weekly physical counts of medicine boxes

explanation: Giving drugs out on 'friendship credit' drains the cash drawer fast, making it impossible to restock. Business and friendly favors don't mix here! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why is balancing the cash register at the end of a shift so important in a DRF unit?

options.A: To prove that the nurses worked longer hours than scheduled
options.B: To ensure that cash collected matches the volume of drugs dispensed
options.C: To decide which drugs are most popular among patients
options.D: To calculate the monthly salary bonus for the nursing staff

explanation: Daily cash reconciliation keeps things transparent, honest, and ensures every single tablet is accounted for. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h6)

question: How does general inflation negatively affect a Drug Revolving Fund over time?

options.A: It causes all tablets inside the store to dissolve faster
options.B: It increases the number of qualified pharmacists available
options.C: It prevents patients from visiting the hospital entirely
options.D: It reduces the purchasing power of the fund over time

explanation: When prices go up everywhere, the cash you have buys fewer replacement drugs than it used to. That's the challenge of inflation! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h7)

question: What smart strategy helps protect a DRF against rising market prices?

options.A: Periodic and responsible review of drug selling prices
options.B: Giving free credit to all patients who request it
options.C: Stopping the purchase of expensive imported medications
options.D: Selling all essential drugs at a 90% discount

explanation: Adjusting prices sensibly helps the fund keep up with replacement costs so the pharmacy never runs dry. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h7)
